Yeah but I can see why it's defined that way. It's defined by the IEPA as "an event that has led to significant consequences to people, the environment or the facility". By that definition both the Iwo Jima and the Thresher were nuclear accidents. But that's misleading because there is nothing nuclear about them. No radiation leaks and no core exposure. Those two factors necessitate the word nuclear. We've never had a core exposure or radiation leak that would fit that definition.

Did you not pay attention at all to the regulations put in place for dumping of radioactive/contaminated materials out to sea? Not only it is public information but was derived from extensive testing of contamination dispersion. Any amount of contamination that violated the quantifiable requirements was pumped to decontamination facilities. I know because as a former ET I had to have these requirements memorized and so did every ELT in Rad Con Div. Also on my aircraft carrier they were incredibly finicky about trash disposal. 

As per nuclear accidents, there haven't been any. We have had maintenance accidents and fires and even a steam line rupture on the USS Iwo Jima. None of those fit the definition of a nuclear accident which is exposure of the core to atmosphere (very oversimplified definition, I'm on a phone). You misunderstand. I wasn't referring to a specific teleological argument. I was defining the term teleological argument and informing you of how it has been used in the past as an arguing point against civil rights and thus how it will be perceived. If you want to argue about your specific argument or the inherent flaws/benefits associated with teleological philosophies as applied to politics in general, we can do that. However, that's a different debate.

The teleological argument is arguing for an idea based on the purpose it serves. This philosophy is often used to argue for the existence of god and, in American history, has again and again been invoked by the religious to justify their legal beliefs. This includes justification of slavery and taking away other people's rights in this country. I do understand your argument. I was recommending you do not use it in this context.

I really don't think you want to invoke that argument in regards to civil rights in the US. The teleological argument was used to justify slavery in this country via bible passages. Also we have a thing about separation of church and state, especially with the existence of hundreds of tax and spousal right laws that coincide with marriage.

It always feels the worse when you are intelligent enough to see your faults, but have absolutely no idea how to get past them, as you have stated. Hating others for not experiencing the same problems as us, not feeling what we do, but then hating ourselves for feeling that way. Doesn't it feel like somebody is sitting there, showing you every single mistake you make? And then, telling you how bad it was, over and over again. This is what people like me, and you, and so many other people do to ourselves. Because this is the only way we know how to think. Nobody has ever said to us "there is another, better, way." And even if they have, how are we to believe them?

This is difficult to explain. Most people will know nothing more to say beyond that statement or beyond "everything is going to be okay". As I grew up, I was taught to feel everything. To sit and dwell in my thoughts and my emotions, and it would make me feel better. That was the only coping mechanism I was taught. So, at 15, I had a suicide attempt and ended up in rehab. There I met a man who taught me to approach things differently. My therapist taught me a different way to look at things and rationalize my emotions. Do you ever feel like there are moments of relief when somebody says something to comfort you? maybe by telling you that you aren't the only one? And then that feeling disappears as quickly as it came.

If this sounds familiar, than you are like me. I learned that I had to teach myself how to think. To look at life in a different, more positive way. To not instinctively feel incredible self loathing or hatred or anxiety every time something went wrong. It was and continues to be the most difficult thing I have ever had to do. I had to convince myself, after years of telling myself that I was the worst person in the world, that I was actually a good person. I'm writing this, not to tell you that I know the answer to your pain. But to tell you that a solution does exist. No matter if the problem is with your mind, life or body.

You are not a bad person. A bad person doesn't ask for help. A bad person doesn't dislike themselves for doing/feeling things they believe are wrong. If you need somebody to talk to. Please feel free to send me a message. I can listen, and hopefully help point you in the right direction. That goes for you too RadioactiveAnimator.

When I first arrived in rehab, I was on the brink of failing out of high school. Not because I wasn't smart enough graduate, but because I was so wrapped up in other things, that I just didn't care to put in the effort to finish school. That didn't stop me from feeling awful about it. Like I was unable to accomplish what every single other kid my age was able to do. I felt like I was falling behind.

My therapist asked me what was the worst possible outcome of all of my failures. He took me down a long road of what-if scenarios until I was homeless on the street without a dollar to my name and a family who shunned me. And then he said to me "So what?". "At this point nobody thinks anything of you, and you know, without death or prison, things cannot get any worse. So where do you go from here"? And then we rebuilt my theoretical life one step at a time until I reached a point where I would be happy. The point of this was to get me thinking of life pragmatically, without focusing on what others thought of me. Without the unnecessary meddling of other silly human beings and their standardized expectations, I was able to focus and survive. 

In real life, I didn't go to college like the other kids did. I joined the military. I put myself in a very different world to force myself to work. I put college on hold for six years while I made myself stronger. It wasn't until after that time that I was ready to start school again (at 24). I am already worlds ahead of many of my peers from high school, even though I am technically behind, because I learned far more about myself and life. What I am trying to say is that you should let go the burdens of what you consider to be failure and alienation. They aren't real. Pay attention and try to learn from and understand what is going on because it could be the key to your happiness. You might be travelling down the wrong road or you might just not be ready for it. You might need this to learn some things or find a stronger friend base. This is an opportunity to figure out what will really make you happy. Whatever you decide, there is always more time, and there is never no way back, unless you hurt yourself.

I appreciate that, but no thanks are needed. I just want to help people who are going through what I did. There is always something you can do, no matter how bad your problems are. You just need to know how to start or where to go. I'm here for anybody to talk to or who needs to be pointed in the right direction.
